notes.meaning: Jesus asked why the mob came with swords and clubs at night when He had taught publicly in the temple courts day after day. Coming in secret showed how cowardly and dishonest their plot was. Yet Jesus willingly allowed Himself to be taken so that the prophecies in Scripture would be fulfilled.

As soon as Jesus surrendered, all of His disciples abandoned Him and ran for their lives. Even though they had promised just hours before to die with Him, fear took over. Their sudden flight fulfilled ancient prophecy that the sheep would scatter when the shepherd was struck.

A young man who was following along was grabbed by the crowd, but he slipped out of his linen cloth and ran away naked. He was likely a neighbor who jumped out of bed when he heard the noisy mob outside. His narrow escape shows how dangerous the arresting crowd was and how completely everyone fled from Jesus.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some note that people in the ancient world sometimes wore only a single linen garment, meaning the young man was not necessarily a sleeper who sprang from bed.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular idea suggests that the young man was a new believer wearing white baptismal clothes when he followed Jesus.

notes.meaning: The crowd led Jesus straight to the palace of Caiaphas the high priest. The chief priests, elders, and teachers of the law all gathered together in the middle of the night for an emergency trial. They held this illegal night meeting because they were determined to condemn Jesus as quickly as possible.

Peter trailed behind Jesus at a safe distance until he slipped inside the high priest's courtyard. Once there, he sat down among the guards and warmed himself by their charcoal fire. By trying to blend in with Christ's enemies, Peter walked straight into the path of temptation.

The high council searched frantically for evidence against Jesus so they could sentence Him to death, but they found nothing. They had already decided on His execution before the trial even began, making the court thoroughly dishonest. Under God's control, not even two witnesses could be found whose stories agreed.

Many people came forward to tell lies about Jesus, but their accusations contradicted each other. God's law required at least two witnesses to agree on the facts before anyone could be put to death. Because their claims did not match, the prosecutors could not build a legal case.

After the earlier attempts failed, a few more men stood up to offer another accusation. They brought up words Jesus had spoken years earlier in Jerusalem to make Him sound like a threat to the nation. They were desperate to find any charge that would stick.

The accusers claimed Jesus boasted that He would destroy the temple and rebuild it without hands in three days. In reality, Jesus had spoken years before about His own body being put to death and raised up again. The witnesses twisted His words to paint Him as a dangerous troublemaker out to destroy their holy building.

Even on this charge about the temple, the witnesses could not get their stories straight. Small differences in how they reported the saying ruined their testimony under the rules of Jewish law. The court was left without any solid ground to condemn Jesus.

Frustrated that the witnesses were failing, the high priest stood up in the middle of the room to confront Jesus. He demanded to know why Jesus stayed silent and refused to answer the charges. He did this in hope of pressuring Jesus into saying something they could use against Him.

Jesus remained silent and gave no reply, showing patient trust in God and fulfilling the prophecy that the Messiah would be quiet before His accusers. The high priest then placed Him under a solemn oath and asked directly if He was the Christ, the Son of God. The title 'the Blessed One' was a respectful Jewish term used to avoid speaking God's holy name aloud.

Jesus answered clearly, 'I am,' openly claiming to be the Messiah and the Son of God. He warned them that they would one day see Him seated at the right hand of God's power and returning on the clouds of heaven as their Judge. He boldly told the truth even though He knew it would result in His death sentence.

Hearing Jesus' words, the high priest tore his clothes in a dramatic display of religious shock. He declared that the council had no further need of other witnesses. By reacting this way, he treated Jesus' honest claim as an obvious crime.

The high priest accused Jesus of blasphemy, which means insulting God, because Jesus claimed divine honor for Himself. He called on the council for their verdict, and everyone present agreed that Jesus deserved to die. Their hatred blinded them to the fact that His claim was true.

Some of the council members and officers began spitting on Jesus, covering His eyes, and punching Him. They mocked Him by demanding that He prophesy who struck Him while blindfolded. Jesus quietly endured this cruel shame, fulfilling the Old Testament prophecy that the Savior would be struck and spat upon.

While the trial was happening on the upper floor, Peter remained below in the open courtyard. A servant girl who worked for the high priest came down into the area where the servants were sitting. Her arrival set the stage for Peter's great test.

The servant girl noticed Peter warming himself as the firelight lit up his face. Looking at him closely, she stated that he had been with Jesus the Nazarene. Her sudden remark dragged Peter out of the shadows and put him on the spot before everyone.

Peter denied it completely, claiming he did not know Jesus or even understand what the girl was saying. Feeling uncomfortable near the fire, he slipped away toward the front entryway, and a rooster crowed. His first denial showed how quickly fear can lead a disciple into lying.

Out near the gate, the servant girl saw Peter again and told the bystanders that he was definitely one of Jesus' followers. She repeated her claim to the whole group gathered there. Peter found that running to another part of the courtyard could not save him from scrutiny.

Peter denied the charge a second time, refusing to stand with his Master. A short time later, the bystanders insisted again that he must be a disciple because his northern accent marked him as a Galilean. Trying to fit into the fireside conversation only ended up exposing him further.

In a panic, Peter began calling down curses on himself and swearing an oath that he did not even know Jesus. He used harsh language so the crowd would believe he was completely unrelated to the prisoner inside. His terror of suffering led him into the deepest point of his fall.

Immediately, the rooster crowed a second time, and Jesus' earlier warning came rushing back to Peter's mind. Realizing that he had denied his Lord three times just as Jesus predicted, Peter broke down in bitter tears. His deep sorrow was the start of true repentance, turning his broken heart back to God.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: An early church interpretation holds that the Greek word means Peter pulled his cloak over his head in shame so he could weep without being seen.
